Work in the smooth category ([[def-smooth-manifold]]). Fix once and for all the
three-sphere as the one-point compactification

$$S^3:=\mathbb R^3\cup\{\infty\}$$

of Euclidean three-space, carrying its standard smooth structure, and fix the
standard orientation of $S^3$: the orientation induced by the standard
orientation of $\mathbb R^3$ under the one-point compactification, so that the
charts of the standard atlas away from $\infty$ are orientation-preserving and
the orientation is that of a connected oriented $3$-manifold in the sense of
[[def-oriented-smooth-manifold-and-oriented-chart]]. For $r>0$ write
$\overline B_r:=\{x\in\mathbb R^3:\lVert x\rVert_2\le r\}$, the closed ball of
[[def-euclidean-spheres-and-closed-balls]] with the following restriction convention. Smoothness on a closed ball means
local extension to a smooth map on an open neighborhood in Euclidean space;
smoothness on $M\times I$, for a smooth manifold $M$ without boundary, means
local extension across $t=0,1$ in $M\times\mathbb R$. Thus these closed domains
are not asserted to be manifolds without boundary in the cited definition.

**Links.** The **standard oriented circle** is the circle
$S^1=\mathbb R/\mathbb Z$ with its standard counterclockwise orientation,
regarded as a smooth $1$-manifold; a
**finite disjoint union of oriented circles** is a smooth manifold
$C=S^1\sqcup\dots\sqcup S^1$ ($k$ summands, $k\in\mathbb N$)
diffeomorphic to the disjoint union of $k$ standard oriented circles. An
**oriented link** (with $k$ components) is a smooth embedding

$$L\colon C\longrightarrow S^3$$

of such a disjoint union in the sense of [[def-smooth-embedding]]. So $L$ is
injective, is an immersion, and is a homeomorphism onto its image with the
subspace topology, and its image $L(C)$ is a finite disjoint union of smoothly
embedded circles. Thus every link considered here is finite and tame: the
smoothness of $L$ is exactly the standing convention, and no polygonal or other
tame model is used. The **components** of $L$ are the images of the individual
summands, and the number of components is $k$.

**Ambient isotopy.** Let $I=[0,1]$. An **ambient isotopy** of $S^3$ is a smooth
map

$$H\colon S^3\times I\longrightarrow S^3$$

such that $H_0=\mathrm{id}_{S^3}$, each $H_t\colon S^3\to S^3$,
$H_t(x):=H(x,t)$, is a diffeomorphism ([[def-diffeomorphism-and-local-diffeomorphism-of-manifolds]]),
and each $H_t$ is orientation-preserving with respect to the fixed orientation.
The last clause is in fact automatic: $t\mapsto H_t$ is continuous in the
$C^\infty$ topology of the diffeomorphism group, the orientation sign is locally
constant in $t$, and $H_0=\mathrm{id}$ is orientation-preserving, so it is kept
only for emphasis.

**Equivalence of links.** Two oriented links $L_0\colon C_0\to S^3$ and
$L_1\colon C_1\to S^3$ are **equivalent** (written $L_0\sim L_1$), or
**ambient isotopic**, when there are an ambient isotopy $H$ and an orientation-preserving diffeomorphism $f:C_0\to C_1$ with
$H_1\circ L_0=L_1\circ f$. Thus parametrizations and component labels are
irrelevant, while the induced orientation of each image component is preserved. The relation is an equivalence relation on links:
it is reflexive with $H=\mathrm{id}$, transitive by composing isotopies, and
symmetric because a smooth family of diffeomorphisms has a smooth family of
inverses. An equivalence class is an **(oriented) link type**.

**Moving off $\infty$.** Because the definition of equivalence allows the
isotopy to move a link through $\infty$, the standard practice of this page is
to first apply an ambient isotopy that carries a given link into the open ball,
and only then to project; every projection and every Reidemeister move below is
read after moving the link off $\infty$ into $\mathbb R^3$ in this way. The
orientation-preserving clause in the definition of ambient isotopy is exactly
what the oriented Reidemeister moves and the oriented closure construction must
respect. The unoriented theory uses the same ambient isotopies but forgets
the orientations of the link components.

**Links in the three-sphere versus links in $\mathbb R^3$.** A link contained in
$\mathbb R^3\subset S^3$ is a link in $S^3$; conversely every link may be
assumed after isotopy to lie in $\mathbb R^3$, by choosing a point outside the compact one-dimensional image and moving that
point to $\infty$ by a smooth rotation of the standard sphere. When comparing
links already in $\mathbb R^3$, an isotopy can also be arranged to avoid
$\infty$ throughout; the track-avoidance argument is given in
[[thm-oriented-reidemeister-equivalence-theorem]].

Let $S\subseteq M$ be an embedded submanifold.

Equip $S$ with the smooth structure supplied by
[[lem-slice-chart-restrictions-form-a-smooth-atlas]]. The inclusion
$i:S\hookrightarrow M$ is then a smooth embedding by
[[prop-the-inclusion-of-an-embedded-submanifold-is-a-smooth-embedding]], so its
differential is defined. Identify $T_pS$ with the linear subspace
$di_p(T_pS)\subseteq T_pM$. Here the notation
$$TM|_S:=\coprod_{p\in S}T_pM,\qquad T^*M|_S:=\coprod_{p\in S}T_p^*M$$
means the fibrewise restriction of these disjoint unions to base points in
$S$; it does not invoke restriction to an open subset.

The **normal-bundle set** of $S$ in $M$ is the fibrewise quotient

$$\nu(S):=\coprod_{p\in S}T_pM/T_pS.$$

The **conormal-bundle set** of $S$ in $M$ is the fibrewise annihilator

$$N^*S:=\{\xi\in T^*M|_S:\xi|_{T_pS}=0\text{ for the base point }p\}.$$

Both are intrinsic constructions attached to the embedding $S\hookrightarrow M$.
The next proposition supplies their smooth vector-bundle structures.

derivations.claim: Use an orientation-preserving identification of the standard three-sphere with the unit sphere in $\mathbb R^4$. Write the knot as $\gamma:S^1\to S^3\subset\mathbb R^4$ and set $\tau(s)=\gamma'(s)/\lVert\gamma'(s)\rVert$. Since $\gamma(s)$ is unit and $\gamma$ is an immersion, $\gamma(s)$ and $\tau(s)$ are orthonormal. The plane $P_s=\{v\in\mathbb R^4:\langle v,\gamma(s)\rangle=\langle v,\tau(s)\rangle=0\}$ is therefore a smooth rank-two subbundle of $TS^3|_K$. Orthogonal projection $v\mapsto v-\langle v,\tau(s)\rangle\tau(s)$ has kernel $\mathbb R\tau(s)$ and image $P_s$, so it identifies this subbundle smoothly with the quotient $\nu_K$ of [F2]. Orient $P_s$ by the rule in the statement.

Cut $S^1$ at one point and fix an oriented local frame on an arc about the cut. Compactness of the remaining interval gives a finite subdivision whose closed subintervals each lie in a bundle-trivializing chart. Inductively extend a frame from one subinterval to the next: on a small overlap, the incoming and chart frames differ by a smooth map into $\mathrm{GL}^+(2,\mathbb R)$. Shrink the overlap so that this map lies in a neighbourhood of its value at the junction where straight interpolation remains in $\mathrm{GL}^+$. Then join that constant value to the identity by a path in $\mathrm{GL}^+$ and use a smooth cutoff to extend the transition across the new subinterval, making the adjusted frame agree on a collar of the junction and be a fixed chart frame away from it. This can be done at each of the finitely many junctions, with the first and last collars expressed in the fixed cut-arc frame by constant matrices. The required paths exist because Gram–Schmidt writes every matrix in $\mathrm{GL}^+(2,\mathbb R)$ as a rotation times an upper-triangular matrix with positive diagonal; rotations are path-connected and the positive-diagonal triangular matrices contract linearly to the identity. We obtain a smooth oriented interval frame with constant transition matrices at its endpoint collars.

Under the endpoint identification, the two endpoint frame germs differ by a constant matrix $A\in\mathrm{GL}^+(2,\mathbb R)$ by step 1.2. Choose a smooth path $B(t)$ from the identity to $A^{-1}$ that is constant on collars of $0$ and $1$, and multiply the interval frame by $B(t)$. The endpoint values and germs now agree under the identification, because the original germs differ by the constant $A$ and $B$ is constant on their collars. The adjusted frame descends smoothly to an oriented frame on $S^1$, giving the required bundle isomorphism.

boundaries.reason: The statement concerns an embedding whose domain is the nonempty circle S^1.
The normal fibres have rank two by the knot-in-three-space hypotheses; no zero-rank case is included.

boundaries.evidence: step 1.1 constructs the rank-two normal plane over each point of the one-dimensional knot.

boundaries.reason: A smooth embedding is an immersion, so its tangent vector never vanishes; the frame construction has no degenerate tangent case.

boundaries.evidence: Steps 1.2 and 1.3 explicitly match the frame germs at the cut endpoints.
Steps 1.2 and 1.3 use finite subdivisions and paths in GL+(2,R), with no choice axiom.

countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

Assume countable choice, as required for the smooth normal-bundle structure in the tubular-neighbourhood interface. Let $K:S^1\to S^3$ be a smooth oriented knot and let $\nu(K)=TS^3|_K/TK$ be its quotient normal bundle. Equip $\nu(K)$ with a chosen smooth fibre norm $\|\cdot\|$. Let $\Phi:\Omega\to S^3$ be a tubular-neighbourhood map from an open neighbourhood $\Omega$ of the zero section in $\nu(K)$ that restricts to the inclusion of $K$. For $\epsilon>0$, define the closed disk subbundle
$$
D_\epsilon\nu(K):=\{v\in\nu(K):\|v\|\le\epsilon\}.
$$
Choose $\epsilon$ so that $D_\epsilon\nu(K)\subseteq\Omega$, and set $N(K)=\Phi(D_\epsilon\nu(K))$. The fibre norm, tubular map, and radius are part of the chosen tubular data. The **exterior** of this chosen tube is
$$
E_K:=S^3\setminus\operatorname{int}_{S^3}N(K).
$$
Retain its boundary $T_K:=\partial E_K=\partial N(K)$, orient $E_K$ by restriction of the fixed orientation of $S^3$, and orient $T_K$ as the boundary of $E_K$. The choice of tubular map and radius is part of the input to this definition.

For every smooth oriented embedding $K:S^1	o S^3$, let $
u_K=K^*TS^3/dK(TS^1)$ be the quotient normal bundle. Orient its two-dimensional fibres so that a positive tangent to $K$ followed by a positive basis of the normal fibre gives the fixed orientation of $S^3$. Then $
u_K$ admits a smooth orientation-preserving bundle isomorphism $
u_K\cong K	imes\mathbb R^2$.

Assume countable choice $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. Let $i:S\hookrightarrow M$ be a closed smooth embedded submanifold. Then there are an open neighbourhood $\Omega\subseteq\nu(S)$ of the zero section in the quotient normal bundle and a diffeomorphism $\Phi:\Omega\to U$ onto an open neighbourhood $U$ of $i(S)$ in $M$, with $\Phi(0_p)=i(p)$ for every $p\in S$. Thus $S$ has a tubular neighbourhood in $M$.

Let $i:S\hookrightarrow M$ be a smooth embedding, and suppose its normal bundle
$\nu(S)$ ([[def-normal-and-conormal-bundles-of-an-embedded-submanifold]]) has
been equipped with its standard smooth-vector-bundle structure. Under
$\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ the existence of this structure is supplied by
[[prop-normal-and-conormal-bundles-are-smooth-vector-bundles]].

A **tubular neighbourhood of $S$ in $M$** consists of:

1. an open neighbourhood $\Omega\subseteq \nu(S)$ of the zero section, and
2. a smooth embedding $\Phi:\Omega\to M$

such that:

- $\Phi(0_p)=i(p)$ for every $p\in S$, and
- $\Phi(\Omega)$ is an open neighbourhood of $i(S)$ in $M$.

Equivalently, $\Phi$ is a diffeomorphism from $\Omega$ onto an ambient open
neighbourhood of $S$, and its restriction to the zero section is the original
inclusion.

derivations.claim: By [F1], $K$ is continuous and $K(S^1)$ is compact because $S^1$ is compact. Since $S^3$ is Hausdorff, $K(S^1)$ is closed; [F1] also identifies it as a smooth embedded submanifold. Thus the closed smooth embedded hypothesis of [F4] holds, and [A1] permits its application. Take a tubular map $\Phi:\Omega\to U\subset S^3$ defined on an open neighbourhood of the zero section of $\nu(K)$.

Use the trivialization [F3] and its product Euclidean norm as the chosen smooth fibre norm in [F2], so $\Omega$ is open in $S^1\times\mathbb R^2$. For each $s\in S^1$, openness gives an arc $I_s$ about $s$ and a radius $r_s>0$ with $I_s\times D^2_{r_s}\subset\Omega$. Compactness of $S^1$ gives a finite subcover by such arcs; taking $\epsilon$ smaller than half the least of their radii yields $S^1\times D^2_{2\epsilon}\subset\Omega$. The closed disk subbundle $S^1\times D^2_\epsilon$ therefore lies in $\Omega$.

Put $N(K)=\Phi(S^1\times D^2_\epsilon)$. The restricted map is a smooth embedding, so $N(K)$ is a compact embedded solid torus with boundary $T_K=\Phi(S^1\times\partial D^2_\epsilon)\cong S^1\times S^1$. Since $S^3$ is compact and $E_K=S^3\setminus\operatorname{int}N(K)$ is closed, $E_K$ is compact. The annulus $S^1\times\{z:\epsilon/2<|z|<2\epsilon\}$ maps to a collar of $T_K$; in these coordinates $E_K$ is the side $|z|\ge\epsilon$. Thus $E_K$ is a smooth three-manifold with boundary exactly $T_K$, oriented by restriction of the orientation of $S^3$ as in [F2].

On $S^3\setminus K$, define $H_t$ to be the identity outside $N(K)$ and, in the punctured disk fibres with $0<|z|\le\epsilon$, set $H_t(\Phi(s,z))=\Phi(s,((1-t)|z|+t\epsilon)z/|z|)$ for $0\le t\le1$. The formula is continuous for $z\ne0$ and is the identity at $|z|=\epsilon$, so it glues continuously to the identity outside $N(K)$. It fixes every point of $E_K$, stays in $S^3\setminus K$, and at $t=1$ sends every point of the punctured tube to $T_K\subset E_K$. Hence $H_t$ is a strong deformation retraction of $S^3\setminus K$ onto $E_K$.

Assume countable choice as in the chosen tubular-neighbourhood data. Let $K$ be a smooth oriented knot with chosen exterior $E_K$ and boundary torus $T_K=\partial E_K$, and let $p:T_K\to K$ be the projection of the chosen normal-disk tube. Orient each normal disk so that its positive tangent direction followed by its oriented normal basis agrees with the orientation of $S^3$. A **meridian** $\mu$ is the oriented boundary of one such normal disk. A **degree-one parallel curve** is a simple closed curve $\lambda$ in $T_K$ for which $p|_\lambda:\lambda\to K$ has degree $+1$. A **preferred longitude** is a degree-one parallel curve satisfying $i_*[\lambda]=0$ in $H_1(E_K;\mathbb Z)$, where $i:T_K\hookrightarrow E_K$ is inclusion. This is a condition on a curve; this definition alone asserts neither existence nor uniqueness. Reversing the orientation of $K$ reverses the orientations of both $\mu$ and any degree-one parallel curve. If a subgroup $P\le\pi_1(E_K,x)$ is specified using a path from $x$ to $T_K$, record it only up to replacing it by $gPg^{-1}$ for $g\in\pi_1(E_K,x)$.

Assume countable choice. For every smooth oriented knot $K$ in $S^3$, there are an oriented normal-bundle trivialization, a tubular map $\Phi$ defined on an open neighbourhood containing $S^1\times D^2_{2\epsilon}$ for some $\epsilon>0$, and a closed tubular neighbourhood $N(K)=\Phi(S^1\times D^2_\epsilon)$. This $N(K)$ is diffeomorphic to $S^1\times D^2$, its boundary $T_K$ is diffeomorphic to $S^1\times S^1$, and its exterior $E_K=S^3\setminus\operatorname{int}N(K)$ is a compact smooth oriented three-manifold with boundary $T_K$. The open complement $S^3\setminus K$ strongly deformation retracts onto $E_K$.

For every CW complex $X$, abelian group $G$, and $n\geq0$, the cellular complex has an
isomorphism $H_n^{\mathrm{cell}}(X;G)\cong H_n(X;G)$, natural with respect to
cellular maps.

Let $X$ be a CW complex, $G$ an abelian group, and $n\geq0$.
The **cellular homology** of $X$ with coefficients in $G$ is
$H_n^{\mathrm{cell}}(X;G)=\ker d_n/\operatorname{im}d_{n+1}$ for the cellular
groups of [[def-oriented-cellular-chain-group]], with differentials defined in
[[def-cellular-boundary-from-three-consecutive-skeleta]].  These maps form a
chain complex by [[lem-the-cellular-boundary-squares-to-zero]].

For $n\geq1$, define $d_n:C_n^{\mathrm{cell}}(X;G)\to C_{n-1}^{\mathrm{cell}}(X;G)$ as the connecting map $H_n(X^n,X^{n-1};G)\to H_{n-1}(X^{n-1};G)$ from [[thm-long-exact-sequence-of-a-pair-in-singular-homology]], followed by the quotient map to $H_{n-1}(X^{n-1},X^{n-2};G)$. Set $d_0=0$.

Let $X$ be a CW complex. For $n\geq1$, in the integral cellular chain groups with the chosen cell orientations,
$$d_ne^n_\alpha=\sum_\beta[e^n_\alpha:e^{n-1}_\beta]e^{n-1}_\beta.$$

derivations.claim: In product coordinates on $T_K=S^1\times S^1$, the meridian $\mu$ is the second factor loop and the section $\sigma$ is the first factor loop. Give the torus its standard product CW structure: take the quotient of a square by identifying opposite edges, with one vertex, the two oriented factor loops as its $1$-cells, and the open square as its $2$-cell attached by the commutator $\mu\sigma\mu^{-1}\sigma^{-1}$.

The cellular chain groups in dimensions $2,1,0$ are $\mathbb Z,\mathbb Z^2,\mathbb Z$. The differential $d_1$ is zero because each $1$-cell starts and ends at the only vertex. By [F7], each coefficient of $d_2$ is the degree of the attaching map after collapsing the other $1$-cell. The commutator traverses each factor once in each orientation, so both degrees are zero. Thus by [F5] and [F6], $H_1^{\mathrm{cell}}(T_K;\mathbb Z)=\mathbb Z^2$ with the factor loops as basis.
By [F4], the same two classes form a basis of singular $H_1(T_K;\mathbb Z)$.

diffeomorphic to the disjoint union of $k$ standard oriented circles. An
**oriented link** (with $k$ components) is a smooth embedding

$$L\colon C\longrightarrow S^3$$

of such a disjoint union in the sense of [[def-smooth-embedding]]. So $L$ is
injective, is an immersion, and is a homeomorphism onto its image with the
subspace topology, and its image $L(C)$ is a finite disjoint union of smoothly
embedded circles. Thus every link considered here is finite and tame: the
smoothness of $L$ is exactly the standing convention, and no polygonal or other
tame model is used. The **components** of $L$ are the images of the individual
summands, and the number of components is $k$.

map

$$H\colon S^3\times I\longrightarrow S^3$$

$H_t(x):=H(x,t)$, is a diffeomorphism ([[def-diffeomorphism-and-local-diffeomorphism-of-manifolds]]),
and each $H_t$ is orientation-preserving with respect to the fixed orientation.
The last clause is in fact automatic: $t\mapsto H_t$ is continuous in the
$C^\infty$ topology of the diffeomorphism group, the orientation sign is locally
constant in $t$, and $H_0=\mathrm{id}$ is orientation-preserving, so it is kept
only for emphasis.

**Equivalence of links.** Two oriented links $L_0\colon C_0\to S^3$ and
$L_1\colon C_1\to S^3$ are **equivalent** (written $L_0\sim L_1$), or
**ambient isotopic**, when there are an ambient isotopy $H$ and an orientation-preserving diffeomorphism $f:C_0\to C_1$ with
$H_1\circ L_0=L_1\circ f$. Thus parametrizations and component labels are
irrelevant, while the induced orientation of each image component is preserved. The relation is an equivalence relation on links:
it is reflexive with $H=\mathrm{id}$, transitive by composing isotopies, and
symmetric because a smooth family of diffeomorphisms has a smooth family of
inverses. An equivalence class is an **(oriented) link type**.

isotopy to move a link through $\infty$, the standard practice of this page is
to first apply an ambient isotopy that carries a given link into the open ball,
and only then to project; every projection and every Reidemeister move below is
read after moving the link off $\infty$ into $\mathbb R^3$ in this way. The
orientation-preserving clause in the definition of ambient isotopy is exactly
what the oriented Reidemeister moves and the oriented closure construction must
respect. The unoriented theory uses the same ambient isotopies but forgets
the orientations of the link components.

assumed after isotopy to lie in $\mathbb R^3$, by choosing a point outside the compact one-dimensional image and moving that
point to $\infty$ by a smooth rotation of the standard sphere. When comparing
links already in $\mathbb R^3$, an isotopy can also be arranged to avoid
$\infty$ throughout; the track-avoidance argument is given in
[[thm-oriented-reidemeister-equivalence-theorem]].
